title: SDK integration walkthrough - Emerald Retail

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-20 15:00 PDT, Duration ~52m. Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Sofia Delgado (Emerald CTO), Marcus Lee (Emerald Lead Engineer), Priya Anand (Emerald DevOps)

00:00 Lena Park (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really quick intro — I'm Lena, AE on the Redwood inference team, with Marco our solutions engineer. Sofia, Marcus, Priya, thanks for making time.
00:12 Sofia Delgado (CTO): thanks, Lena, excited to see the SDK flow, we've been evaluating a couple providers but want to see how quick we can get a POC running in our stack.
00:20 Marco Ruiz (SE): Awesome. Agenda: quick tour of console, then live runthrough of the Python and TypeScript quickstarts, auth flow (API keys vs SSO), then Q&A and next steps. We'll also touch on Dedicated and Private (VPC) options since you mentioned latency SLOs in the form.
00:45 Marcus Lee (Lead Engineer): Great, our primary constraints: sub-200ms p95 on short prompts, and cost under a certain threshold. We do a lot of small chat completions and some embeddings for search.
01:05 Marco Ruiz (SE): Got it. Quick note: we'll show the hosted API for fastest setup, and then outline Dedicated and Private options for predictable throughput and VPC. For SDKs, we support Python and TypeScript—pip package or npm package.
01:25 Lena Park (AE): I'll drop the quickstart links in the chat. 
01:35 Marco Ruiz (SE): Alright jumping into console — you should see the model catalog, routes, and keys. For quickstarts the standard pattern is set env var REDWOOD_API_KEY then call the SDK. For Python it's pip install redwood-inference, import RedwoodClient, and client.generate(...). For TypeScript npm i @redwood/inference, import { Redwood } from '@redwood/inference' and use client.chat.create.
02:10 Marcus Lee: Quick Q — how are API keys scoped? Can we rotate them automatically and do per-route keys?
02:20 Marco Ruiz: Yes, keys can be scoped to routes and you can rotate via the console or API. We also integrate with SSO/SAML for user access, and for service-to-service you can mint short-lived tokens via our token service if you want more ephemeral creds.
02:45 Priya Anand (DevOps): We have strict KMS/HSM rules for keys at rest, is that supported?
02:56 Marco Ruiz: We support customer-managed keys via KMS for Private deployments; for Hosted we encrypt at rest with provider-managed KMS but can offer BYOK for enterprise contracts — we'll include the security pack with details.
03:20 Lena Park (AE): I'll include SOC2 and ISO docs after the call.
03:30 Sofia Delgado: Perfect.
04:00 Marco Ruiz (SE): Ok switching to code — I'll share my screen, running through the Python quickstart. Note: transcription may mangle code words a bit — the snippet is in the GH repo.
04:15 Marco Ruiz (SE): (screen) Terminal: python -m venv venv; source venv/bin/activate; pip install redwood-inference. Then in app.py: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')); resp = client.generate("Summarize this text..."); print(resp.text) — that's the simple flow.
05:05 Marcus Lee: Sounds straight forward. How do we stream tokens for low-latency UI?
05:15 Marco Ruiz: We support SSE and WebSocket streaming in both SDKs; for JS/TS you can use the streaming client that emits tokens as they arrive, same pattern in Python with the async iterator. That helps hit interactive latency SLOs while batching in the back end.
05:45 Marcus Lee: What's the default batching behavior? Could batching push some requests over your 200ms SLO?
06:00 Marco Ruiz: The runtime is workload-aware; it does continuous batching but has latency cutoffs. You can configure per-route SLOs; if latency priority is high we'll favor smaller batches or dedicated capacity. This is where Redwood Optimize comes in — it will suggest batching windows and quantization to hit cost targets without breaking latency.
06:40 Sofia Delgado: Can you summarize Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private implications?
06:48 Lena Park (AE): Hosted = fastest for POC, lowest ops; Dedicated = reserved GPU pools for your org with predictable throughput and better latency guarantees; Private = VPC or on-prem for regulated data, gives you control over networking and KMS. Costs increase along that line but predictability and security controls also increase.
07:20 Priya Anand: If we do Private, can we still use Redwood's control plane? We want customer-managed network but not all the ops.
07:31 Marco Ruiz: Yes, we offer a private deployment option where the control plane can be hosted or customer-managed; we can talk specifics in the architecture doc.
07:45 Marcus Lee: Ok moving on to TypeScript demo please.
07:52 Marco Ruiz: (shares) npm i @redwood/inference; in ts: import Redwood from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const stream = await client.chat.stream({ messages: [...] }); stream.on('token', t => renderToken(t));
08:30 Marcus Lee: For embeddings — do you have a simple batch endpoint? We batch hundreds of texts nightly for search indexing.
08:40 Marco Ruiz: Yes, embeddings endpoint supports batching and auto-retry; we also provide a bulk ingestion helper in the SDK and recommend using the dedicated pool for sustained high throughput. We'll share our batching best practices doc.
09:00 Sofia Delgado: Any E2E latency numbers for typical 2k token generation on hosted?
09:10 Marco Ruiz: Typical p95 for short prompts is 80-160ms on hosted for small models; larger generation will be higher. We'll provide model performance profiles from our catalog for the models we demo.
09:40 Marcus Lee: Who's the point of contact if we run into infra issues during POC?
09:48 Lena Park: Marco will be SE lead, Lena will be account AE. We'll also bring in solutions engineering if we need deeper kernel/quantization tuning.
10:00 Marco Ruiz: Back to auth, quick note on env vars: we recommend REDWOOD_API_KEY for service apps, store in secret manager and for CI use short-lived tokens. For browser clients, route through your backend to avoid leaking keys.
11:00 Priya Anand: About network egress — how does traffic flow for hosted? Does traffic to Redwood go over the public internet?
11:12 Marco Ruiz: Hosted uses public endpoints; for Private we can establish VPC peering or private networking. There are options for private-link style connections depending on cloud provider.
11:40 Marcus Lee: Ok good. Now on instrumentation — how do we trace requests back to our code?
11:48 Marco Ruiz: We include request IDs in responses and have hooks for tracing; you can pass a correlation id per request, and our Console shows per-route latency and cost. We also export logs for audit.
12:15 Sofia Delgado: Are there rate limits on trial keys?
12:20 Lena Park: Trials have soft limits; for benchmark runs we can lift them temporarily. We'll coordinate that in next steps.
13:00 Marco Ruiz: Alright I'm going to run a small live example — I'll hit the hosted endpoint with a short prompt, watch the streaming tokens, and then show the same call using a dedicated route configured with higher priority.
13:20 Marco Ruiz: (exec) // streamed output — you'll see tokens come in; console shows token-level cost and latency breakdown.
14:10 Priya Anand: I saw KV cache in the UI, can you explain the cache behavior?
14:20 Marco Ruiz: Sure, the KV cache (sometimes called K V cache in auto-transcripts) stores prefix activations for recent sessions to speed up repeated context. It's configurable per route; for high QPS chat apps it massively reduces per-token compute.
14:50 Marcus Lee: Any problems with cache staleness when we roll models?
15:00 Marco Ruiz: We have cache invalidation controls on rollouts — you can flush per route or set TTLs. During canary rollouts we route some traffic to the new model and keep caches isolated per model version.
15:45 Sofia Delgado: Security/Compliance — can you support audit logs sent to our SIEM?
15:55 Marco Ruiz: Yes audit logs can be exported via syslog or S3 export; for enterprise customers we can set up push to your SIEM.
16:20 Lena Park: I'm adding the security pack link (redwood.com/security-pack) in chat after the call.
16:35 Marcus Lee: Ok, can you share sample load test config?
16:42 Marco Ruiz: We'll share a JMeter/locust script in the quickstart repo and we can coordinate a benchmark window.\17:00 Sofia Delgado: What about cost controls — can we cap spend per route?
17:08 Marco Ruiz: Yes you can set quotas and alerts per route, and Redwood Optimize suggests quantization and batching changes for cost reduction. Optimize also flags quality regressions against your evals.
17:40 Priya Anand: About quantization — do you do int8 support in the runtime?
17:48 Marco Ruiz: We support several quantization profiles, including int8 and mixed precision paths; recommendation depends on model and latency targets. Marco: we'll run some quantized runs during the benchmark.
18:15 Lena Park: Quick objection we hear often: other vendors offer simpler pricing but opaques performance. How do you usually respond?
18:25 Marco Ruiz: We emphasize production economics — transparent token-level cost, model performance profiles, and the Optimize suggestions so you can see the tradeoffs clearly.
19:00 Marcus Lee: Anything about network egress charges from your side?
19:08 Marco Ruiz: Egress depends on cloud provider; for Dedicated we can place inference in your region to minimize egress. We'll map out cost expectations in the spreadsheet.
19:40 Sofia Delgado: Alright let's talk timeline — we want a POC in two weeks, then decide on Dedicated in 4–6 weeks. Is that realistic?
19:50 Lena Park: Yes, two-week POC for a functional integration is common. We'll provide trial keys and the quickstart repo today.
20:05 Marcus Lee: Ok good.
20:30 Marco Ruiz: I'm pasting GH repo link now (github.com/redwood-inference/quickstarts) and the TypeScript sample path. Also linking the batching best practices doc and the model performance sheet.
21:00 Priya Anand: Noted. A couple more infra questions: NAT gateway requirements, firewall rules, outbound ports?
21:10 Marco Ruiz: For hosted you need HTTPS outbound to api.redwood.com; for private you may need specific peering and firewall rules — we'll add a checklist to the repo.
21:40 Sofia Delgado: Do you support regional model placement? We need EU residency for some customers.
21:50 Marco Ruiz: Yes we have model hosting in multiple regions and can pin model execution to EU regions for data residency. We'll note region options in the spreadsheet.
22:20 Marcus Lee: Ok any gotchas for TS type definitions? We use strict TS and like typed responses.
22:30 Marco Ruiz: SDK returns typed objects and we include TypeScript definitions; for structured outputs you can use the function-calling or schema features to get typed payloads.
23:00 Lena Park: Quick poll — are you leaning hosted first for POC?
23:05 Sofia Delgado: Yes hosted for POC.
23:10 Marcus Lee: Hosted for POC, Dedicated if performance looks good.
23:20 Priya Anand: Same.
23:30 Marco Ruiz: Great. Wrapping up demo portion — sample links and artifacts will be shared.
24:00 Marco Ruiz: (recap) We'll provide: quickstart repo, pricing + Dedicated options sheet, security pack, batching best practices, and schedule benchmark run.
24:20 Lena Park: Any final questions?
24:30 Sofia Delgado: Can you include sample SAML metadata for SSO setup?
24:35 Marco Ruiz: Yes we'll include SAML metadata and SSO setup guide.
24:45 Marcus Lee: For benchmarking — we run 500 RPS simulating many small chat messages; will you be able to support that in trial?
24:55 Lena Park: We'll coordinate and temporarily raise trial limits for the benchmark window.
25:10 Priya Anand: Thanks.
25:20 Marco Ruiz: One more note — when you run the TypeScript sample, set the environment variable REDWOOD_API_KEY and REDWOOD_ENV=staging for the trial keys we'll provision.
25:40 Lena Park: I'll send calendar invite for the benchmark slot.
26:00 Sofia Delgado: Great.
26:15 (longer discussion about internal stakeholders and procurement)
30:00 Sofia Delgado: procurement question — do you have standard enterprise contracts?
30:10 Lena Park: Yes, we have standard MSA and addenda for data residency and privacy; legal can start once scope is confirmed.
31:00 Marcus Lee: Ok.
32:00 (minor cross talk and clarifications)
40:00 Marco Ruiz: Going back to the KV cache note — devs often confuse it with session cache; clear naming docs in repo.
42:00 Sofia Delgado: appreciated.
45:00 Priya Anand: We'll assemble an internal checklist and share in the next couple days.
47:00 Lena Park: Perfect. Thanks everyone for your time.
47:10 (quick final clarifications, confirming who will do what)
51:30 Lena Park: End of call — recap in email and next steps as discussed.

End of transcript.
